newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA wants small Superfund law changes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA wants small Superfund law changes.

text.p: The Clinton administration Wednesday urged Congress to make small, targeted changes in the Superfund toxic waste cleanup law, despite complaints from many Republicans that the current law is fatally flawed.

"Legislative reform must build on the administrative improvements to the program and must be narrowly targeted to address critical issues in need of a legislative solution," Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Carol Browner said in a letter to the Senate Environment Committee.
She said administrative changes have resulted in a toxic waste cleanup program "fundamentally different from the Superfund program of four years ago."
After several years of failing to reach an agreement, Congress again is trying to reauthorize the Superfund law, which has been criticized for generating more lawsuits than cleanups of toxic sites.
A spokesman for Rep. Mike Oxley, chairman of a key House Commerce subcommittee, said there were no surprises in the EPA's position.

"I don't know that there's anything at all that new about it, but aside from that, Mr. Oxley is going to hold off commenting until after a briefing" later Wednesday, the spokesman for the Ohio Republican said.
The EPA called for clearly defined limitations or exemptions on liability but stressed that polluters who were responsible for contamination should pay for cleanup.

The EPA said legislation is needed to establish separate funding for "orphan shares" of insolvent or defunct parties and to promote settlements and a more flexible allocation of costs among parties through better use of orphan shares.
The agency opposes eliminating liability based upon the type of site, repealing strict retroactive liability standards, and pre-empting state liability laws.

It also opposes prescriptive cost or risk assessment requirements and other changes that it said would result in inadequate cleanups and opposed capping recoverable damages or limiting natural resources that could be restored.
